The early life history of Spisula subtruncata begins with the release of fertilised eggs that develop into free-swimming veliger larvae. The wet weight of a newly hatched individual is exceedingly small, measured at 0.000000097 grams [Wwb = 0.000000097 grams], which corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 57 micrometres. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth is just 3 days [ab = 3 days], a brief period that reflects the rapid embryogenesis typical of many planktotrophic bivalves. Following hatching, the yolk-sac larva soon exhausts its endogenous reserves and commences active feeding on phytoplankton, marking the onset of exogenous feeding. This planktonic stage persists for several weeks as larvae drift in the water column, growing and developing the velum that facilitates both locomotion and particle capture. The prodissoconch shell expands steadily during this period, and larvae eventually undergo a dramatic morphological transformation known as larval settlement, which involves the loss of the velum and the initiation of gill development. The time since birth at metamorphosis has been recorded as 24 days  at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], after which the newly metamorphosed spat settle onto the substrate.

Once the post-metamorphic juvenile has settled, it enters a phase of rapid somatic growth, gradually increasing its shell dimensions. A critical life history milestone is the attainment of sexual maturity, which occurs when an individual reaches a shell length at puberty of 1 cm [Lp = 1 cm]. This measurement is accompanied by a corresponding shift in body composition, with the ashfree dry weight at puberty reaching 0.02 grams . In terms of age, the time since birth at puberty is achieved after 180 days [tp = 180 days] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This developmental schedule is comparatively accelerated relative to some larger congeners, reflecting the relatively moderate ultimate shell height of 3.5 cm [Li = 3.5 cm] that defines the maximum size attainable by this species. The progression from metamorphic spat to a reproductively viable organism therefore occupies a substantial portion of the first half-year of life, with growth rates that are strongly modulated by local food availability and water temperature.

Reproductive investment in Spisula subtruncata can be quantified through gonadal mass measurements taken from individuals of varying body sizes. At a standard temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the ashfree dry gonadal mass at 0.05 grams of total ashfree dry weight (AFDW) equals 0.014 grams . For a larger individual with a total AFDW of 0.13 grams, the corresponding gonadal mass is 0.030 grams , reflecting a proportional increase in reproductive tissue as somatic mass accumulates at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. At the upper end of the sampled size range, specimens with a total AFDW of 0.17 grams exhibit a gonadal mass of 0.038 grams  at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This progressive increase in gonadal tissue with body size suggests that fecundity is positively correlated with somatic mass, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous bivalves that allocate additional resources to reproduction as they grow. The gonadal mass values reported here were derived from dissections of individuals collected during the peak spawning season and processed for ashfree dry weight determination following standard protocols.

Total lifespan in Spisula subtruncata has been documented using field surveys of marked cohorts and analysis of shell growth rings. The maximum recorded longevity is 4 years [am = 4 years], a value established under natural thermal conditions averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is consistent with the species' status as a fast-growing, early-maturing bivalve that occupies unstable sandy habitats subject to frequent disturbance from storms and sediment transport. Mortality in older individuals is often attributed to senescence, during which physiological deterioration and reduced feeding efficiency lead to a gradual decline in condition. Comparisons with other members of the family Mactridae indicate that the lifespan of S. subtruncata is typical for small-bodied surf clams, whereas larger congeners such as Spisula solidissima may persist for over a decade. The 15 °C [T = 15 °C] isotherm used in these longevity estimates corresponds closely to the mean annual water temperature across much of the species' geographic range in the northeastern Atlantic.

The ecological context of S. subtruncata is shaped by its role as a suspension feeder in shallow subtidal sand flats, where it contributes to benthic-pelagic coupling. Population dynamics are strongly influenced by recruitment success, which depends on the timing of spawning relative to phytoplankton blooms. The relatively brief planktonic larval duration of 24 days  at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] ensures that competent pediveligers are available to settle during periods of favourable substrate availability. Individuals that reach the ultimate shell height of 3.5 cm [Li = 3.5 cm] are typically among the oldest in the population, having successfully avoided predation by demersal fish and crustaceans throughout their lives. The species exhibits a typical bivalve life cycle in which external fertilisation produces zygotes that develop through trochophore and veliger stages before undergoing metamorphic settlement. The 3 day [ab = 3 day] age at birth at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] ensures rapid development through the most vulnerable early embryonic stages, while the 180 day [tp = 180 day] interval to puberty at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] allows sufficient time for the accumulation of somatic reserves necessary to support gametogenesis.
